topic.title: CI/CD Pipelines — quality gates, immutable releases and rollback

outcomes: Design CI pipelines that validate code, data, model, prompt and container artifacts before release.
Build once and promote the same immutable image digest through environments.
Separate test, build, signing, approval and deployment identities using least privilege.
Define security, quality, latency, cost and compatibility gates for AI releases.
Implement sequential environment promotion with idempotency, audit events and canary rollback.
Explain branch protection, artifact retention, environment approvals, provenance and release evidence.
prerequisites: Git, branches, pull requests and automated tests
Docker image build and supply-chain security
Stage 9 Topics 1–5: experiment tracking, model registry, evaluation CI, data pipelines and containers

glossary.definition: Continuous Integration: automatically validate changes through builds, tests, static analysis and policy gates.
Continuous Delivery/Deployment: package and promote validated artifacts; deployment applies them to an environment.
A versioned build output such as a container image, model, prompt bundle, dataset manifest or SBOM.
A content-addressed artifact identifier that pins exact bytes, unlike a mutable tag.
Evidence describing source, builder identity, workflow, dependencies and parameters used to create an artifact.
Software Bill of Materials listing packages and components in a release artifact.
A measurable rule that must pass before an artifact can advance to the next release stage.
Repository-hosted controls such as required reviewers, wait timers and deployment branch restrictions.
Expose a small percentage of traffic to a candidate, compare health/SLOs and increase or roll back.
Maintain two production environments and switch traffic after the inactive environment passes checks.
Restore a previously validated artifact/configuration when the candidate violates a release or runtime policy.
A structured assurance framework for describing and strengthening software build integrity.

explanation.problem: Passing unit tests is not enough to release an AI service. A model can be accurate but unsafe, an image can contain a vulnerable dependency, a prompt can break structured output, a dataset can be incompatible, and a deployment can exceed latency or cost budgets. CI/CD connects all these checks into a controlled release process.
explanation.plainLanguage:
CI starts when code or a pull request changes. A strong pipeline checks formatting and types, runs unit and integration tests, validates data contracts, evaluates prompts/models against a fixed golden set, checks security and licensing, builds a container, generates an SBOM, scans the image and records provenance. A failed required gate blocks the candidate. Do not allow a workflow to silently skip a check because an optional secret or external service is unavailable.

Build once, promote many. Build the container and model/prompt bundle once from a known commit and record immutable digests. Development, staging and production should receive the same artifact bytes. Rebuilding separately for each environment means different dependencies, timestamps or build arguments can produce different artifacts even when the tag looks the same. Keep environment-specific configuration outside the image and bind it to a versioned release record.

A release candidate is more than an image tag. It includes source commit, image digest, model and prompt versions, dataset manifest, evaluation report, SBOM, vulnerability report, signature and build provenance. A promotion gate checks that these records agree and are approved. For an AI workload, also check quality, safety, p95 latency, error rate, cost per successful task and feature/schema compatibility.

Use least-privilege workflow permissions. Pull-request CI normally needs read-only repository access. Package publication needs package-write permission only in the release job. Signing should use a dedicated identity and short-lived OIDC credentials rather than long-lived private keys in repository secrets. A deploy identity should be separate from a build identity. Avoid checking out untrusted fork code in a privileged job that has secrets or write permissions.

Promotion should be sequential and explicit. Development proves the artifact can run. Staging proves compatibility with production-like configuration and data. Production requires an independent approver and a measured rollout. GitHub Environments can enforce reviewer approval and branch restrictions, but application policy must still validate who is allowed to promote which release. Approval must bind to the exact digest and release metadata, not merely a branch name.

Canary rollout exposes a small traffic slice, such as 1–5%, and watches task success, safety violations, error rate, p95/p99 latency, saturation and cost. Increase traffic only when thresholds hold for a sufficient window and sample size. If an SLO is breached, stop the rollout and restore the previous known-good digest. Rollback should restore all coupled components: application image, model, prompt, feature definitions, retrieval index version and configuration. Record the failed release and reason in an append-only audit trail.

A CI/CD system should be idempotent and recoverable. Retrying a release event must not create duplicate deployments or overwrite a previous artifact. Use a stable release ID and idempotency key. Store immutable release records, approvals and audit events. Keep artifacts long enough to reproduce and roll back supported releases. A green pipeline is evidence that gates passed; it is not a guarantee that production will remain healthy. Runtime observability and incident response remain essential.
explanation.mentalModel: Commit → tests + data/model eval + security → build once → SBOM + signature + provenance → immutable candidate → dev → staging approval → production canary → promote or rollback.
limitations: A green CI run does not prove runtime behavior under all workloads.
Golden-set evaluations can be overfit; maintain representative, versioned and independently reviewed data.
Vulnerability scanners do not prove exploitability or absence of vulnerabilities.
A signature proves artifact identity/attestation under a trust policy, not that the model is safe or accurate.
Canary metrics need sufficient traffic and time; low-volume services require careful statistical interpretation.
Rollback may require coordinated schema, feature, index and database compatibility rather than switching only an image.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: A pharmaceutical batch cannot be shipped just because the factory machine ran. It needs batch records, lab results, packaging inspection, independent release approval, traceability and a recall plan. CI/CD applies the same idea to software and AI artifacts.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: Suppose a canary receives 5% of 20,000 requests: 1,000 candidate requests. If 30 fail, observed error rate is 3%, above a 2% budget, so halt and roll back. For latency, compare candidate p95=920 ms with the release limit 800 ms. Do not average away a breached slice or combine unrelated cohorts; compare like-for-like traffic and account for sample size and confidence.
explanation.productionImpact: Immutable artifacts and provenance support audits; evaluation/security gates block unsafe candidates; independent approvals reduce privilege risk; canaries detect regressions before full traffic; coordinated rollback restores a known-good system state.

useCase.scenario: A pull request changes an inference API. CI validates Python, contract tests and a golden evaluation, builds one image, generates SBOM and scans it. A release candidate is promoted to dev, staging and production using the same digest. A 5% production canary breaches the error budget, so the pipeline restores the previous image/model/prompt bundle and records the reason.
constraints: Pull-request jobs use read-only permissions by default.
Release artifact is built once and referenced by immutable digest.
Promotion requires signed provenance and quality/security evidence.
Staging and production approvals are independent.
Canary must meet error, latency, safety and cost budgets.
Rollback restores the complete compatible release bundle.
outputs: Rollback event and restored release identity
useCase.successMetric: Every production release can be traced to a source commit and verified artifact digest; an injected canary regression automatically halts promotion and restores the previous known-good release.

dataFlow.purpose: Run unit, integration, type, security, data and AI evaluation tests.
Build one candidate image and bundle.
Generate SBOM, scan and sign provenance.
Promote exact artifact through dev and staging.
Observe quality, safety, latency, error and cost.
Increase traffic or restore previous known-good bundle.

trustBoundaries: Fork PRs and user-controlled workflow inputs are untrusted.
Workflow token permissions are scoped per job and environment.
Build identity, package publisher, signer and deployment identity are separated.
Approvals are bound to immutable release ID and digest.
Artifact registry and audit log enforce immutability and retention.
Runtime telemetry is authenticated and sampled without leaking user payloads.
failurePaths: Unit or AI evaluation failure: stop before image publication.
Critical vulnerability: block release and require patched rebuild or reviewed exception.
Artifact tag drift: reject tag-only release and require digest.
Approval replay or stale release: bind approval to release ID, digest and environment.
Canary SLO breach: halt traffic ramp and restore prior release bundle.
Partial rollback: verify model/prompt/feature/index compatibility and restore coordinated versions.
Workflow compromise: revoke identity, rotate credentials, audit published digests and rebuild from trusted source.

workedExample.problem: Promote release r1 through environments and simulate a failed production canary.
workedExample.input: Candidate passes tests, signature, provenance, scan, quality=.96, p95=350ms and cost=$0.25/1k. Production canary sees 30 errors in 1,000 requests.

steps.reasoning: All release evidence meets configured policy thresholds.
Bind one image digest and SBOM to release r1.
Require engineer and release-manager roles, respectively.
30/1000 = 3%, above the 2% error budget; p95 is 920ms above 800ms.
Switch production alias to r0 and append a rollback event.

workedExample.expectedOutput: The release is stopped at 5% traffic and production returns to the previous known-good digest.

failures.name: Tests pass but AI quality regresses
failures.symptom: Application deploys with a prompt/model change that lowers task success or safety.
failures.rootCause: Pipeline only tests application code and omits golden-set evaluation.
failures.recovery: Make model/prompt evaluation a required release check and bind its report to candidate digest.
failures.regressionTest: Inject a quality score below floor and assert promotion is denied.

failures.name: Build once, deploy different bytes
failures.symptom: Staging and production tags resolve to different images.
failures.rootCause: Pipeline rebuilds per environment or promotes mutable tags.
failures.recovery: Build once, record immutable digest and promote that digest unchanged.
failures.regressionTest: Reject tag-only candidates and assert digest remains identical across environments.

failures.name: Privileged pull request workflow
failures.symptom: Untrusted fork code can access package-write token or signing credentials.
failures.rootCause: Secrets and write permissions are exposed to pull-request jobs.
failures.recovery: Use read-only PR permissions and separate protected release jobs with short-lived identity.
failures.regressionTest: Static policy test checks PR workflow permissions and job separation.

failures.name: Approval replay
failures.symptom: An old approval is reused for a new image or different environment.
failures.rootCause: Approval is not bound to release ID, digest, target and expiry.
failures.recovery: Bind approval to immutable candidate metadata and enforce one-use idempotent promotion.
failures.regressionTest: Attempt to promote changed digest with same release ID and reject.

failures.name: Canary regression ignored
failures.symptom: Traffic ramp continues while error rate or p95 breaches SLO.
failures.rootCause: No automated canary analysis or thresholds are too broad.
failures.recovery: Stop ramp on breached error/latency/safety/cost policy and restore previous release.
failures.regressionTest: Inject 3% errors against 2% threshold and assert rollback.

failures.name: Partial rollback
failures.symptom: Image rolls back but model, prompt or feature schema remains incompatible.
failures.rootCause: Release record versions only the application container.
failures.recovery: Promote and rollback a complete release bundle with compatibility metadata.
failures.regressionTest: Reject a rollback bundle whose model or feature versions are incompatible.

scenarioQuiz.question: Why should one image digest be promoted through environments?
options: It makes environments identical by magic
It guarantees the same artifact bytes are tested and released
It removes the need for approvals
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Build once and promote the same immutable digest to avoid environment rebuild drift.

scenarioQuiz.question: What permissions should ordinary pull-request CI have?
options: Read-only by default, with separate protected release permissions
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Untrusted pull request code should not receive privileged release credentials.

scenarioQuiz.question: A 5% canary has a 3% error rate against a 2% budget. What should happen?
options: Ignore because only 5% traffic is affected
Stop the rollout and restore the previous known-good release
scenarioQuiz.explanation: A canary gate should halt and rollback when an agreed SLO is breached.

scenarioQuiz.question: What should an AI release bundle pin?
options: Image, model, prompt, feature/data and configuration versions with provenance
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Rollback and compatibility require coordinated version references across coupled artifacts.

rubric.criterion: CI validation and AI quality gates
rubric.evidence: Tests, data contracts, golden evaluation and security checks are required.
Build once, digest, SBOM, signature and source provenance are bound.
PR, publisher, signer and deploy identities have separated permissions.
Sequential environment gates require role-specific approval and idempotency.
SLO breach halts ramp and restores complete known-good bundle.

evidence: Candidate cannot promote with missing or failed evidence.
Promotion is sequential, role-bound and idempotent.
CI workflow sample does not deploy or publish by default.

codeWalkthrough.explanation: A release candidate binds source and immutable artifacts to test, security and AI evaluation evidence.
A release gate aggregates all failed policy reasons. Promotion is denied if tests, security, quality, latency or cost do not pass.
Promotion checks candidate identity, target environment, role and replay protection before changing the environment alias.
Canary metrics are compared with explicit budgets. A breach restores the previous known-good release.
The sample workflow builds and scans a candidate without publishing or deploying it. A separate protected release workflow should handle promotion.
Repository environment protection can require reviewers and restrict branches, but the release service must still validate digest-bound approval.
